lesson.title: Cells, rows and formulas
lesson.subtitle: Cell addresses, ranges, formulas, and a Python list

video.title: Cells, rows and formulas
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — the computer studies teacher (main character)

scenes.visual: Icon cards: 40 numbers; 3 answers; A better way. Mr Joseph beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Zainab added up her class's marks with a calculator. Forty numbers, three times, and three different answers! There's a better way.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card: the Darsi mark, the course name and the lesson title with the Data engineering track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: spreadsheets, formulas, and your first lines of Python.

scenes.visual: One big value: B2, Column B, row 2.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A spreadsheet is a big table. Columns have letters: A, B, C. Rows have numbers: one, two, three. So every cell has an address, like B2: column B, row two.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: =SUM(B2:B9): adds a range; =AVERAGE(B2:B9): the mean; =COUNTIF(C2:C9,"P"): matches.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A formula starts with an equals sign. SUM of B2 to B9 adds up eight cells: a range. AVERAGE finds the mean, and COUNTIF counts the cells that match.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: Updates by itself; No new mistakes; Needs a tidy table.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: And when a mark changes, the formula updates by itself. No adding up again, and no new mistakes. But it only works if the table is tidy: one value in each cell.

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! What does SUM of B2 to B5 add up?

scenes.visual: Icon cards: B2; B3; B4; B5.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: B2, B3, B4 and B5: the colon means everything from B2 to B5. That's called a range.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: marks = [12, 15, 9, 18] … Caption: Prints 54, then 13.5
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Programs can do this too. In Python, a list holds the marks in square brackets. sum adds them up, and len counts them. Divide one by the other, and you have the average.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: “14 / 17”: text, can't add; A Total row: a fake pupil; Tidy: one value per cell.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Formulas and programs both need tidy data. A mark typed as fourteen slash seventeen is text, and text can't be added. A Total row inside the data gets counted as a pupil.

scenes.visual: Icon cards joined by arrows: 3 wrong answers; One tap at a time; All right.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the app, Mr Bello's marks sheet gets three questions wrong. Fix the table one tap at a time, and watch the computer's answers turn right.

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Why is a formula better than typing the total yourself?

scenes.visual: Summary card: Every cell has an address; Formulas: = and a range; They update by themselves; Python: sum and len. Takeaway bar: Let the formula do the adding.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: It updates by itself when a mark changes. Remember: every cell has an address, like B2. Formulas start with equals, and work on ranges. And in Python, sum and len do the same job.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: A week of something; Total and average; Change one, watch. Mr Joseph beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: make a table of something you track for a week, like hours of sleep. Add a total and an average with formulas. Then change one number, and watch them update.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — B2:B5 is a range: every cell from B2 to B5.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the colon means “from … to”, so B2:B5 is B2, B3, B4 and B5.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is a formula better than typing the total yourself?

options.text: It updates when a mark changes

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — change a mark, and the total and average update with no new mistakes.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a formula recalculates by itself when the data changes, so the total is always right.
